lines.text: Coal, steam, iron and cotton. In little more than a century, Britain and then the world moved from hand work to machines. This is how it happened.
It begins in 1709, when the ironmaster Abraham Darby smelted iron with coke instead of charcoal, and cheap iron became possible.
Three years later came the steam engine, using the push of steam to drive a piston. It would power mines, mills, trains and ships.
Thomas Newcomen's engine was the first practical one, built to pump water out of coal mines. It burned fuel greedily, but it spread across Britain.
In Birmingham, the manufacturer Matthew Boulton would later team up with James Watt and sell their steam engines to the world.
Richard Arkwright, born in 1732, would build great water-powered cotton mills, with workers on fixed shifts, a model for industry.
In 1733 John Kay's flying shuttle let a single weaver make wide cloth twice as fast.
James Watt, a Scottish instrument maker, added a separate condenser that made the steam engine far more efficient. The unit of power still bears his name.
By around 1760 the great change was under way: from farms and hand work to factories, steam power and crowded new cities.
In 1761 the Bridgewater Canal began carrying coal to Manchester, and the price of coal there fell by half.
Then the spinning jenny let one worker spin several threads at once, speeding up cotton making in homes across Britain.
In Birmingham, inventors and thinkers such as Watt and Wedgwood met to dine on full moon nights, sharing the ideas of the age.
Arkwright's water frame needed a water wheel to drive it, and so it needed mills. The factory system had begun.
Robert Owen, born in 1771, would run his mill village at New Lanark with schools and shorter hours, an early socialist dream.
That same year Arkwright opened his mill at Cromford in Derbyshire, often called the first true factory.
In 1776 Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations, explaining how specialised work, trade and competition make a nation rich.
In 1779 the Iron Bridge spanned the River Severn at Coalbrookdale, the first major bridge made of cast iron, and a symbol of the new age.
The same year Samuel Crompton's spinning mule spun fine, strong thread, and the cotton boom took off.
George Stephenson, born in 1781, would become the father of railways and choose the track gauge most of the world still uses.
Edmund Cartwright's power loom of 1785 brought machines to weaving, and in time put hand weavers out of work.
In America the cotton gin made cotton cheap to clean, raising demand for the crop, and tightening the grip of slavery in the South.
Isambard Kingdom Brunel, born in 1806, would build railways, bridges, tunnels and great ships on a grand scale.
Not everyone welcomed the machines. From 1811 the Luddites, textile workers whose wages were cut, smashed them in protest.
In Essen that same year, Friedrich Krupp founded a firm that would grow into a German giant of steel, railways and guns.
Charles Dickens was born in 1812. His novels would expose the poverty and injustice of industrial Britain.
After 1815 the Corn Laws taxed foreign grain to protect landowners, keeping bread dear for the poor for thirty years.
In 1818 Karl Marx was born in Germany. He would argue that the struggle between classes drives history.
In 1819 cavalry charged a vast crowd in Manchester demanding the vote, killing at least fifteen people. It became known as Peterloo.
In America, the Erie Canal linked the Hudson River to the Great Lakes, and helped make New York the nation's leading port.
That same year in north-east England, the Stockton and Darlington became the first public railway to use steam locomotives.
In 1829 Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill Trials. Its many-tubed boiler set the pattern for steam locomotives for a century.
The next year the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, with every train on steam and a timetable. The railway age had arrived.
In 1833 a Factory Act banned children under nine from textile mills, with inspectors to see it was obeyed.
A year later six farm workers were sent to Australia for forming a union. Protests won their return, and they became heroes of the labour movement.
Meanwhile German states formed a customs union, the Zollverein, which helped Germany industrialise and, in time, unite.
In Scotland, Andrew Carnegie was born. In America he would build a steel empire, then give his fortune away to fund libraries.
By 1837 the electric telegraph was sending messages along wires, cutting news from days to minutes.
The Chartists marched for votes for all men and a secret ballot. Their petitions were refused, but most of their demands later became law.
In 1843 Brunel launched the SS Great Britain, a giant iron ship driven by a propeller across the Atlantic.
The same year, the Brunels' Thames Tunnel opened in London, the first tunnel under a river that ships could sail on.
Then came Railway Mania, as investors rushed into railway shares. Many lost their savings, but thousands of miles of track were built.
In America, Thomas Edison was born in 1847. His laboratory would bring the phonograph, the light bulb and electric power.
In 1848 Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto, calling on the workers of the world to unite.
In 1851 the Great Exhibition filled the Crystal Palace in London with the machines of the world, and millions came to see them.
Three years later, cholera struck Soho. The doctor John Snow traced it to a single water pump, and its handle was removed.
In the mid fifties, Henry Bessemer found a way to blow air through molten iron and make steel cheaply, for rails, ships and buildings.
In 1858 a cable was laid across the Atlantic seabed. It failed within weeks, but by 1866 a lasting link carried news in minutes.
That hot summer the Thames stank so badly of sewage that London finally built its great network of sewers.
In 1868 Japan's shogun fell and power returned to the emperor. The Meiji Restoration set Japan racing to build its own industry.
In 1869 a golden spike in Utah completed America's first railroad from coast to coast, turning months of travel into a week.
The same year the Suez Canal opened, joining the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and cutting the route to Asia by thousands of kilometres.
In 1870 John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil, which came to control most American refining, until the courts broke it up.
In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone, and voices began to travel along wires.
Around 1879, Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison each made a practical light bulb, and night began to change.
In 1884 Charles Parsons built his steam turbine. Turbines like it still make most of the world's electricity.
Then came the war of the currents: Edison's direct current against the alternating current of Westinghouse and Tesla. Alternating current won.
And in 1908 the Model T rolled out, soon built on a moving assembly line. More than fifteen million brought motoring to ordinary families.
From a coke furnace to the assembly line, the machine age had remade how the world lives and works.
